notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on 2 Samuel 15, drawn from the approved sources.

---

## 2 Samuel 15 — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### v. 1 — Absalom’s Chariot and Runners
**“Some time later, Absalom provided for himself a chariot with horses and fifty men to run ahead of him.”**

- **Traditional Reading:** The Hebrew phrase “after this” implies Absalom began his plotting soon after being restored to court (Pulpit). The chariot and fifty runners were a display of regal pomp — the first such use in Israel — and a tacit claim to kingship, just as Adonijah later did (1 Kings 1:5) (Ellicott, Gill). Absalom was creating an image, a “man of the people” persona, though he was actually positioning himself above others (Enduring Word).
- **Reformed / Evangelical:** Thomas Constable notes this was part of a four-year plan to undermine confidence in David, the Lord’s anointed, through military display and image-crafting (Constable). Precept Austin calls it “Absalom’s version of a Porsche” — for show, not speed.
- **Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/ ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-15.html ; https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-samuel-15-commentary

---

### v. 2 — Standing at the Gate
**“He would get up early and stand beside the road leading to the city gate. Whenever anyone had a grievance to bring before the king for a decision, Absalom would call out and ask, ‘What city are you from?’…”**

- **Traditional Reading:** The “gate” was that of the royal palace where David held audience and administered justice as the “supreme court” of the kingdom (Pulpit, Enduring Word). David did hold court — the woman of Tekoa obtained an audience — so Absalom’s interception of suitors was a calculated act of sedition. The Pulpit Commentary suggests David’s administration of justice had become “half-hearted” because of his own guilt over adultery and murder, leaving a gap Absalom exploited (Pulpit). Absalom’s question “What city are you from?” showed a personal interest that was politically calculated (Enduring Word).
- **Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/ ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/15.htm

---

### vv. 3–4 — “Your claims are good and right, but the king has no deputy…”
**“Look, your claims are good and right, but the king has no deputy to hear you… If only someone would appoint me judge in the land…”**

- **Traditional Reading:** Ellicott notes Absalom used the classic demagogue’s tactic: he never directly attacked the king, but insinuated the *system* was defective. There was indeed an official hearer appointed (Jehoshaphat and Seraiah, 2 Sam 8:16–17), but David’s moral “malady” had let the system weaken (Pulpit). By telling each litigant his case was “good and right,” Absalom flattered individuals while sowing discontent (Pulpit, Gill). Guzik observes that Absalom left troubled people *more* troubled than when he found them (Enduring Word).
- **Reformed / Baptist:** Constable notes this was a promise to rule better than David, part of Absalom’s patient, four-year scheming (Constable).
- **Sources:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-15.html

---

### v. 5 — The Hand and the Kiss
**“When anyone approached to bow down to him, Absalom would reach out his hand, take hold of him, and kiss him.”**

- **Traditional Reading:** Absalom refused to let others bow to him; instead he lifted them up, shook their hand, and kissed them — projecting a “man of the people” image. Guzik comments that Absalom didn’t actually consider himself a man of the people; he knew he was better-looking, better-connected, and had better instincts, but his political savvy told him to fake common touch (Enduring Word). The kiss, combined with his personal beauty, made his affability “charming and irresistible” (Pulpit).
- **Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/ ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/15.htm

---

### v. 6 — “Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel”
**“Absalom did this to all the Israelites who came to the king for justice. In this way he stole the hearts of the men of Israel.”**

- **Traditional Reading:** Gill says Absalom gained the people’s affections “in a private and clandestine manner, and robbed the king of them, who had the best right unto them” (Gill). Guzik lists the reasons Israel’s hearts were stolen: David was aging; his sins diminished his standing; people like change; Absalom was skilled and cunning; and David had to “enter into the fellowship of His sufferings” like the Son of David would later be rejected (Enduring Word).
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** The Ligonier devotional notes that Absalom’s coup “shocked David back to reality” after his long spiritual lethargy following the Bathsheba affair (Ligonier, via search excerpt).
- **Sources:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/ ; https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/david-flees-jerusalem

---

### v. 7 — “After four years” (Textual Issue)
**“After four years had passed, Absalom said to the king, ‘Please let me go to Hebron to fulfill a vow I have made to the LORD.’”**

- **Textual Issue:** The Hebrew text reads “forty years,” which is chronologically impossible since David’s entire reign was 40½ years and Absalom was born during it. The Syriac, Vulgate (most MSS), and Josephus read “four years,” which is almost universally accepted by the commentators consulted (Ellicott, Pulpit, Constable, Gill). The four years are probably reckoned from Absalom’s return to Jerusalem (Ellicott) or his reconciliation with David (Gill).
- **Traditional Reading:** Hebron was Absalom’s birthplace, a holy city from ancient times, David’s first capital — and its people may have resented the transfer of the capital to Jerusalem, making them receptive to Absalom (Ellicott, Constable). The vow may have been real or fictitious; either way, Absalom used it as a “cloak of religion” to veil treason (Ellicott, Pulpit).
- **Sources:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-15.html

---

### vv. 8–9 — The Vow and “Go in Peace”
**“For your servant made a vow while dwelling in Geshur of Aram… ‘Go in peace,’ said the king.”**

- **Traditional Reading:** David’s “Go in peace” were his last words to Absalom — deeply ironic. The Pulpit Commentary suggests David’s confidence and lack of suspicion were the result of “noble-minded generosity.” He may even have been pleased at this indication of religious feeling in his son, looking on the better side of Absalom’s acts (Pulpit). Guzik notes that divisive people rarely see themselves as divisive; they cast themselves as crusaders for God’s righteous cause (Enduring Word).
- **Sources:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/

---

### v. 10 — Spies and the Trumpet
**“Then Absalom sent spies throughout the tribes of Israel with this message: ‘When you hear the sound of the horn, you are to say, “Absalom reigns in Hebron!”’”**

- **Traditional Reading:** The “spies” were actually emissaries sent to disperse throughout the land, ready to spread the proclamation once the trumpet sounded at Hebron. The Pulpit Commentary explains that the trumpet was heard only at Hebron, but the news would rapidly spread, and these agents, knowing the plan in advance, would turn rumor to Absalom’s advantage (Pulpit). Absalom counted on the hope that most would see this as succession, not treason (Enduring Word).
- **Sources:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/

---

### vv. 11–12 — The 200 Guests and Ahithophel
**“Two hundred men from Jerusalem accompanied Absalom. They had been invited as guests and they went along innocently… he sent for Ahithophel the Gilonite, David’s counselor…”**

- **Traditional Reading:** The 200 men were prominent Jerusalem citizens, invited to the sacrifices and entirely ignorant of the plot. Absalom needed them to give his cause the appearance of legitimacy — either they would join him, or be forcibly prevented from opposing him, and in any case their presence made it seem they endorsed him (Ellicott, Enduring Word). Guzik remarks: “When the innocent and unknowing are among the divisive, their silence is always received as agreement” (Enduring Word).
- **Ahithophel:** His defection cut David deeply (see Psalm 41:9). He was Bathsheba’s grandfather (2 Sam 11:3; 23:34), and his motive may have been bitterness over David’s sin against his granddaughter (Constable, Enduring Word). Ellicott notes an alternative view: Ahithophel and other Judeans may have resented their diminishing importance as David’s empire grew (Ellicott). His presence “made the conspiracy strong” — he was renowned for his near-prophetic wisdom (2 Sam 16:23) (Enduring Word). His treachery and suicide make him a type of Judas Iscariot (John 13:18) (Ellicott, Pulpit).
- **Sources:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-15.html

---

### vv. 13–14 — David Flees
**“Then a messenger came to David and reported, ‘The hearts of the men of Israel are with Absalom.’ And David said… ‘Arise and let us flee…’”**

- **Traditional Reading:** David’s decision to flee was wise: Ahithophel and Hushai both later recognized that delay would be fatal to Absalom’s cause (2 Sam 17). David spared Jerusalem from a siege and the “edge of the sword,” and gave time for reflection to turn men back to him (Ellicott, Bridgeway). Constable notes David was fleeing from an attack, not going into exile, and planned to return (Constable). The Pulpit Commentary observes that David’s humiliating flight brings out “all the better parts of the king’s character,” and the psalms written at this time (3, 4, 41, 55, 61, 62, 63) show firm confidence in God despite panic and grief (Pulpit).
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** The Ligonier devotional says Absalom’s coup “shocked David back to reality” — from this point on, “the old David, the pious and wise leader of God’s people, was mostly back” (Ligonier excerpt).
- **Sources:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-15.html ; https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/david-flees-jerusalem

---

### vv. 15–16 — Servants’ Loyalty and the Ten Concubines
**“The king’s servants replied, ‘Whatever our lord the king decides, we are your servants.’ …he left behind ten concubines to take care of the palace.”**

- **Traditional Reading:** The servants modeled true service by offering unconditional obedience (Constable). David left ten concubines to “keep the house,” thinking they could safely remain. Guzik notes this reveals David had at least ten concubines — legal mistresses — showing he “sometimes indulged his passions instead of restraining them in a godly way” (Enduring Word). Tragically, these women would later be violated by Absalom publicly (2 Sam 16:21–22), fulfilling Nathan’s prophecy (2 Sam 12:11).
- **Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-15.html

---

### vv. 17–18 — The Last House and the Foreign Bodyguard
**“He stopped at the last house, and all his servants marched past him — all the Cherethites and Pelethites, and six hundred Gittites who had followed him from Gath.”**

- **Traditional Reading:** “The last house” (Beth-merhak, “the Far House”) was probably a pavilion on the outskirts of Jerusalem where David mustered his forces before crossing the Kidron (Pulpit, Ellicott). The Cherethites and Pelethites were David’s bodyguard; the 600 Gittites were not Philistines but the veteran warriors (“Gibborim,” the “mighties”) who had followed David since his outlaw days (1 Sam 22:2; 27:2), later forming his elite corps — compared by one commentator to “Napoleon’s Old Guard” (Pulpit). Constable adds that ancient kings preferred foreign bodyguards since they were unlikely to be swayed by local politics (Constable).
- **Sources:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-15.html

---

### vv. 19–20 — David to Ittai: “Go back”
**“Why should you also go with us? Go back and stay with the new king, since you are both a foreigner and an exile from your homeland. In fact, you arrived only yesterday…”**

- **Traditional Reading:** Ittai was a recent arrival from Gath, a foreigner with no stake in Israel’s internal affairs. David’s use of “the king” for Absalom shows he was willing to let go of the throne and leave matters with God; he did not speak ironically (Ellicott). David released Ittai from any obligation, showing magnanimity (Ligonier). MacLaren is quoted by Guzik: “Remember, the more rebels there are, the more need for us to be conspicuously loyal to our King” (Enduring Word).
- **Reformed / Baptist:** Constable compares Ittai’s commitment to Ruth’s words to Naomi (Ruth 1:16–17) (Constable). F.B. Meyer highlights David’s “thoughtfulness of Ittai” amid his own sorrow (Meyer, via search excerpt).
- **Sources:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-15.html

---

### vv. 21–22 — Ittai’s Vow
**“As surely as the LORD lives, and as my lord the king lives, wherever my lord the king may be, whether it means life or death, there will your servant be!”**

- **Traditional Reading:** Ittai meant David, not Absalom, when he said “my lord the king.” His loyalty was decisive, voluntary, public, and costly — he came to David “yesterday” yet pledged everything. Guzik quotes Spurgeon: “If Ittai, charmed with David’s person and character, though a foreigner and a stranger, felt that he could enlist beneath his banner for life… how much more may you and I, if we know what Christ has done for us… plight our troth to Him” (Enduring Word). Constable notes David later made Ittai commander of a third of his army (2 Sam 18:2) (Constable).
- **Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-15.html

---

### v. 23 — Weeping and Crossing the Kidron
**“Everyone in the countryside was weeping loudly as all the people passed by. And as the king crossed the Kidron Valley, all the people also passed toward the way of the wilderness.”**

- **Traditional Reading:** The “countryside” denotes the inhabitants watching the king’s departure; “the people” are David’s retinue (Pulpit). The general lamentation shows David was not actually unpopular in Jerusalem (Pulpit). The Kidron Valley lies immediately east of Jerusalem, between the city and the Mount of Olives (Ellicott). David’s movement across the Kidron and up Olivet anticipated the path of his descendant Jesus during His passion (John 18:1) (Constable, Enduring Word). Guzik quotes Spurgeon: “Ah! We do not like going over Kedron… how we struggle against suffering, and especially against dishonour and slander!” (Enduring Word).
- **Sources:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-15.html ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/

---

### vv. 24–26 — The Ark Returned
**“Zadok was also there, and all the Levites with him were carrying the ark… David said, ‘Return the ark of God to the city. If I find favor in the eyes of the LORD, He will bring me back… But if He should say, “I do not delight in you,” then here I am; let Him do to me whatever seems good to Him.’”**

- **Traditional Reading:** This is the theological high point of the chapter. David refused to treat the ark as a talisman or good-luck charm (unlike Eli’s sons in 1 Sam 4:3) (Constable, Ellicott). His words show “complete submission to God’s authority” (Constable), “devout resignation and trust” without superstition (Pulpit). David recognized he was suffering the punishment pronounced by Nathan and threw himself entirely into God’s hands (Ellicott). Guzik calls this “active, not passive, trust” (Enduring Word).
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** “David was not willing to have the ark leave its designated city. His charge to the priests shows a remarkable surrender to the providence of God… That is the kind of faith the leader of God’s people should have. After being absent for so long, the man after God’s own heart had returned” (Ligonier excerpt).
- **Baptist / Evangelical:** F.B. Meyer calls it “an impressive picture of the resignation of a broken and a contrite heart” (Meyer, via search excerpt).
- **Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/ ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-15.html ; https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/david-flees-jerusalem

---

### vv. 27–29 — David’s Spy Network Begins
**“Are you not a seer? Return to the city in peace — you with your son Ahimaaz, and Abiathar with his son Jonathan. See, I will wait at the fords of the wilderness until word comes…”**

- **Traditional Reading:** Zadok is called a “seer” (prophet) — David recognized his supernatural insight would be useful (Enduring Word, Ellicott). By sending the priests back, David established an intelligence network in Jerusalem. “The fords of the wilderness” probably refers to the Jordan River fords near the wilderness of Judah, a strategic location allowing quick retreat across the Jordan if needed (Constable, Ellicott). The priests’ sons, Ahimaaz and Jonathan, would serve as couriers (Bridgeway).
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** David “showed wisdom and a good understanding of providence. He knew the Lord would work things out… but that did not mean he had to sit back and passively watch things unfold. Our wise planning and trusting in the Lord’s providence are not opposed” (Ligonier excerpt).
- **Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/ ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-15.html ; https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/david-flees-jerusalem

---

### v. 30 — David on the Mount of Olives
**“But David continued up the Mount of Olives, weeping as he went up. His head was covered, and he was walking barefoot. And all the people with him covered their heads and went up, weeping as they went.”**

- **Traditional Reading:** The covered head and bare feet were standard emblems of mourning and shame (Constable, Enduring Word). Walking barefoot symbolized “the shameful exile on which he is now embarking” (cf. Isaiah 20:2–3; Micah 1:8) (Constable). G. Campbell Morgan is quoted: “In light of all the facts it is almost certain that the tears David shed as he climbed Olivet, were rather those of humiliation and penitence, than those of self-centered regret” (Enduring Word). MacLaren adds: “He is crushed by the consciousness that his punishment is deserved — the bitter fruit of the sin that filled all his later life with darkness” (Enduring Word).
- **Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-15.html

---

### v. 31 — Ahithophel’s Betrayal and David’s Prayer
**“Now someone told David: ‘Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom.’ So David pleaded, ‘O LORD, please turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness!’”**

- **Traditional Reading:** This short prayer is one of the most significant in the chapter — God answered it through the provision of Hushai (vv. 32–37). David knew Ahithophel’s counsel was near-infallible (2 Sam 16:23). Guzik notes this was a prayer born of deep personal pain: Ahithophel was David’s trusted friend, and his betrayal may have been motivated by what David did to Ahithophel’s granddaughter Bathsheba (Enduring Word).
- **Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/ ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/15.htm

---

### vv. 32–34 — Hushai the Archite
**“When David came to the summit, where he used to worship God, Hushai the Archite was there to meet him with his robe torn and dust on his head. David said to him, ‘If you go on with me, you will be a burden to me. But you can thwart the counsel of Ahithophel for me if you return to the city…’”**

- **Traditional Reading:** The summit of the Mount of Olives had a place of customary worship, likely a “high place” (Ellicott). Hushai’s arrival in mourning clothes was the beginning of God’s answer to David’s prayer in v. 31 (Ellicott, Enduring Word). David’s plan was to place Hushai as a mole inside Absalom’s court.
- **Ethical Issue (v. 34):** Ellicott is direct: “David here counsels fraud and treachery… The narrative simply states the facts without justifying them.” However, Ellicott adds two mitigating points: (1) such stratagems have been practised in all ages during war and rebellion; (2) David and Hushai “had but slender knowledge of the Divine revelation of truth and righteousness which enables us to condemn them” (Ellicott).
- **Reformed (Ligonier):** God answered David’s prayer “not by striking Ahithophel directly. Instead, he provided Hushai the Archite, whom David commissioned to be his man on the inside” (Ligonier excerpt).
- **Sources:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/ ; https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/david-flees-jerusalem

---

### vv. 35–36 — The Spy Network Detailed
**“Will not Zadok and Abiathar the priests be there with you? Report to them everything you hear from the king’s palace. Indeed, their two sons… are there with them. Send them to me with everything you hear.”**

- **Traditional Reading:** David organized a complete intelligence chain: Hushai would gather information inside Absalom’s court, relay it to the priests Zadok and Abiathar, and their sons Ahimaaz and Jonathan would carry messages to David at the fords of the wilderness (Bridgeway, Constable). This is David at his best — combining faith in God’s sovereignty with shrewd, practical action (Ligonier).
- **Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-15.html ; https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/david-flees-jerusalem

---

### v. 37 — Hushai Enters Jerusalem as Absalom Arrives
**“So David’s friend Hushai arrived in Jerusalem just as Absalom was entering the city.”**

- **Traditional Reading:** The timing is providential — Hushai enters Jerusalem at the very moment Absalom does, positioning him perfectly to offer his services without suspicion (Pulpit, Enduring Word). The Pulpit Commentary notes Absalom had “evidently pushed rapidly forward from Hebron, in hopes, perhaps, of surprising David in the city” (Pulpit). The stage is set for the counsel-war of 2 Samuel 16–17.
- **Sources:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/ ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/2_samuel/15.htm

---

## Tradition-Specific Notes

### Reformed / Presbyterian
The **Ligonier** devotional (https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/david-flees-jerusalem) emphasizes God’s sovereignty and providence throughout: David’s surrender of the ark demonstrates trust in God alone, not in religious objects. David’s planning (the spy network) and trust in providence “are not opposed” — true trust acts wisely. The devotional also frames Absalom’s rebellion as God’s chastening that finally awakened David from spiritual lethargy.

### Baptist
**F.B. Meyer** (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/fbm/2-samuel-15.html) focuses on David’s broken and contrite heart: “David was conscious of ill desert… Ah, conscience doth make cowards of us all! And yet there was a beautiful spirit of resignation welling up amid the salt waves of his bitter sorrow.” Meyer finds in David’s words (“let him do to me as seemeth good to him”) a model for believers passing through dark hours.

### Pentecostal / Charismatic
**David Guzik at Enduring Word** (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-samuel-15/) combines pastoral application with attention to Absalom’s political cunning and David’s spiritual recovery. He highlights the work of grace in David’s heart — David’s sin was “ever before him,” and in a “strange combination of deep gratitude and horror over his forgiven sin, David never did it again.” Guzik also applies Ittai’s loyalty directly to Christ-devotion, quoting Spurgeon at length.

### Evangelical
**Thomas Constable** (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-15.html) reads the chapter through the lens of leadership and friendship: Absalom is the negative example; Ittai, Zadok, Abiathar, and Hushai are the positive models of costly loyalty. Constable also notes typological parallels between Absalom’s rebellion against God’s anointed and the Jews’ rejection of Jesus.

---

## Other Views

### Textual Criticism (v. 7)
The Hebrew Masoretic Text reads “forty years,” but the **NET Bible** notes (referenced via studylight.org sources) and virtually all commentators consulted agree the original was “four years.” The evidence: the Syriac, Arabic, most Vulgate manuscripts, and Josephus all read “four.” The number forty is chronologically impossible — Absalom was not yet forty when he died, and David’s entire reign was only 40½ years. The confusion likely arose from a scribal error between the Hebrew words *arbaim* (forty) and *arba* (four).
- **Sources:** https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_samuel/15.htm ; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-samuel-15.html

### Catholic / Orthodox
No distinctively Catholic or Orthodox commentary on this chapter was located within the approved search sites (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org). The Catholic Encyclopedia at newadvent.org and Catholic Answers at catholic.com did not return relevant verse-by-verse material for 2 Samuel 15 in the available searches. The **Orthodox Church in America** site (oca.org) also did not yield chapter-specific commentary in the searches conducted.

### Modern Scholarship
No specific articles on 2 Samuel 15 were found at bibleodyssey.org in the searches conducted. The **NET Bible** notes (netbible.org) were not directly accessible in the searches, though Constable’s commentary references textual and scholarly notes throughout.
